heroLead: Van Horn is the Culberson County seat, sitting at the far western reach of the Delaware Basin where the Apache and Beach Mountains start to break up the flat basin floor.
intro: This is quieter country than Reeves or Ward counties to the east. Culberson County has real Wolfcamp and Bone Spring potential, but development here has been more selective, and ranching still dominates the local economy more than oilfield work does. If your family's minerals are near Van Horn, that western-edge position matters for what a fair valuation looks like.

sections.heading: Western edge, not the busy core
paragraphs: Culberson County sits at the transition where the Delaware Basin's dense development starts to thin out, giving way to the mountain terrain further west. Some sections have seen horizontal drilling; a lot of the county remains held by older, quieter leases or simply undrilled. We check current permits near your specific tract rather than assuming activity based on the broader Delaware Basin's reputation.

sections.heading: Ranching-family ownership going back generations
paragraphs: Much of the land around Van Horn has stayed in large ranching operations for a long time, and mineral ownership here often traces back to those original family holdings, sometimes with fractional interests split among heirs who've since scattered across the country.

sections.heading: What it means to sit on the edge of the play
paragraphs: Owners near Van Horn sometimes assume that because they're not in the middle of the Delaware Basin's busiest counties, their minerals have little value. That's not automatically true — edge-of-play acreage can still see meaningful development as operators extend units outward from denser areas, and even undeveloped minerals can carry real value based on that future potential.
